title: Chalcedon, 451
hookLine: one person in two natures; the Oriental Orthodox did not accept it, and recent dialogues found more agreement than feared

cards: Bethany, outside a tomb. A man named Lazarus has been dead four days. His sisters are grieving, the neighbors weeping, and John's Gospel says, in three short words: "And Jesus wept."
Real tears, from a real friend. A few verses later, the same man stands at the same tomb and calls out, "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man walks out.
One person: tears in one moment, a voice that empties a grave in the next. How do you say who that is? Bishops meeting at Chalcedon tried to put it into words.

teach.h: ONE PERSON. HOW DO THE TWO BELONG?
teach.b: Ephesus had said Christ is one person. The next question was how his divinity and his humanity belong together in that one person. Did the human dissolve into the divine, like a drop of honey in the sea?
Or were there really two, side by side?

The Catechism gives Chalcedon's answer, from 451: one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division or separation.
Four withouts. Without confusion: the human isn't swallowed by the divine. Without change: neither stops being what it is.
Without division, without separation: there aren't two Christs. The one who wept at the tomb and the one who called Lazarus out are not two people taking turns. Now the hard part.

A family of ancient churches did not accept Chalcedon's wording: among them the Coptic Church of Egypt, the Armenian Apostolic Church, and the Syriac and Ethiopian Orthodox churches, together called the Oriental Orthodox churches.
They preferred to speak, with Cyril of Alexandria, of one nature of the Word made flesh, and they heard in two natures a risk of splitting Christ in two.
Chalcedon's defenders heard in one nature a risk of swallowing his humanity.
Each side, some historians say, feared the worst of the other.
In our own time, popes have signed common declarations with Coptic and Armenian patriarchs, saying together that Christ is perfect God and perfect man, one Christ. The old formulas still differ.
The agreement underneath turned out larger than either side feared.

how: Catholics confess Chalcedon's teaching in the Creed's 'true God from true God' and 'became man'; the Catholic Church holds official dialogues with the Oriental Orthodox churches, and popes have signed common declarations with Coptic and Armenian patriarchs.

games.q: you're at Chalcedon. one side says Christ's humanity melts into his divinity. another seems to make him two. how do you say it?
o: one person in two natures, without confusion or separation.
games.why: Chalcedon: one and the same Christ, truly God and truly man, in two natures without confusion, change, division or separation.

practice: Bring to mind a Coptic or Armenian church, or simply the people who worship in them, praying today to the same Christ who wept at Lazarus's tomb.

If you pray, pray for them and for full communion between their churches and Rome; if you don't, hold them with good will. Then let the Bethany story run once more, slowly: the tears, and then the voice at the tomb.

wordCard.voice: Chalcedon. The council that confessed Christ as one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion and without separation. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: two natures, one christ. Tears, and a voice that empties a grave, from one person. See you tomorrow.
